doc.title: John LaPorta interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 13, 1996

chapter: Race, feel and playing with Mingus
title: Playing with Charles Mingus and loosening the time
summary: Mingus freed him to play, moved the time around, and older drummers disliked it.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Well it’s served you pretty well. I’m interested in, you brought up Charles Mingus and I know you did some significant work with him, in fact we have this piece of work here. And you got along pretty well with him then.

Yes, that was the only time we ever had a rub. But getting along with Mingus well can be a problem too because he was the kind of person who was always looking for your Achilles heel, and I didn’t like being thought of in that way. I just wanted to make music together. But I loved playing with him. I felt like he took the handcuffs off and made me free to play. Because a lot of rhythm players didn’t care about playing with him because his approach was quite different. He was playing less like just a timekeeper, you know just the basic function is to play the quarter notes and keep steady time. And he played, well he moved the time around you know and the rhythm sections are much more fluid today, and he was one of the influences toward that end.
Yeah, he was in on it early. It must have been hard to play with that unless you really could free up.

Well drummers didn’t like it, especially the older drummers didn’t like that because they came from a different school and they felt most comfortable, people have a tendency to build their own yards and exclude anything that happens after their time you know. And it’s sort of rigor mortis sets in then you know.
